claims.statement: Jim Clark was born at Kilmany on 4 March 1936 and grew up at Edington Mains in the Scottish Borders. The Jim Clark Trust describes a childhood shaped by farm work and driving farm vehicles. Racing did not replace an established junior-formula career: it developed alongside a life in which farming had originally been the expected occupation.

evidence.locator: The Early Years: birth, move to Edington Mains, return to farming and driving vehicles

claims.statement: His progression through sports cars and Formula Junior brought him into Colin Chapman’s Lotus team in 1960. The partnership became the constant of his Formula 1 career: every championship victory in Clark’s record was taken in a Lotus. Changes in engine and chassis followed, but he did not pursue his titles by moving between rival constructors.

evidence.locator: Early racing, Lotus Elite/Formula Junior and promotion to Team Lotus in 1960

claims.statement: Clark’s first championship win came at the 1962 Belgian Grand Prix. Further wins in Britain and the United States made him a title contender, but the championship went to Graham Hill. The distinction between winning races and winning a season is particularly visible here: Clark’s breakthrough year ended with three victories and second place in the final standings.

claims.statement: In 1963 the balance changed decisively. Clark won seven championship races and took his first world title. His success stretched from Belgium through the closing South African round.

evidence.locator: 1963: seven race wins, Belgium through South Africa; final positionNumber=1; exact driverId/id=jim-clark; see statistics-assertions.json for typed checks and archive-validation.json for executed record hashes

claims.statement: John Surtees took the 1964 title; Clark returned to the top in 1965. That second championship included wins in South Africa, Belgium, France, Britain, the Netherlands and Germany. He missed Monaco while competing at Indianapolis.

evidence.locator: 1964 and 1965 final standings; six 1965 wins; no Monaco 1965 race-result row; exact driverId/id=jim-clark; see statistics-assertions.json for typed checks and archive-validation.json for executed record hashes

claims.statement: At Indianapolis Clark drove the Lotus-Ford to victory after leading 190 of the 200 laps. He had already finished second there in 1963 and would do so again in 1966. The Speedway’s own account places the 1965 result within the wider move toward rear-engined cars, rather than treating Clark’s win as the work of one driver in isolation.

evidence.locator: Race Stats: 1963, 1965 and 1966 rows; 1965 Led=190, Laps=200
Rear-engine transition, Ford, Chapman and Wood Brothers contributions

claims.statement: The next championship did not repeat that pattern. In 1966 Clark won only the United States Grand Prix while Jack Brabham became champion. His long Lotus partnership therefore contained both commanding seasons and less productive ones.

evidence.locator: 1966 winning results; Brabham final championship position; exact driverId/id=jim-clark; see statistics-assertions.json for typed checks and archive-validation.json for executed record hashes

claims.statement: The Lotus 49 and Cosworth DFV made their winning championship debut at Zandvoort in 1967 with Clark driving. Classic Team Lotus records the new three-litre engine and the car’s subsequent victories with him. Clark won four championship races that season and opened 1968 with another victory in South Africa, again in the Lotus.

evidence.locator: Introduction at Zandvoort in 1967; first Cosworth DFV 3-litre engine and Clark victories

claims.statement: Graham Hill was now Clark’s Lotus team-mate, not simply an opponent from the BRM years. Clark won four championship races in 1967, while Denny Hulme took the title for Brabham.

claims.statement: Gerald Donaldson’s Formula 1 profile describes Clark compensating for an imperfect car and relying on Chapman to turn his comments into engineering changes. The partnership combined the driver’s feel for the car with the designer’s technical direction. It continued through changing Lotus chassis and engines, from the early Formula 1 years to the DFV-powered car of his final season.

evidence.locator: Paragraph after the 1965 championship: Chapman translating feedback and Clark driving around problems

claims.statement: Clark won the opening South African Grand Prix of 1968, taking his world-championship total to 25 victories. It was also his last Formula 1 start.

claims.statement: On 7 April 1968 Clark was killed during a Formula 2 race at Hockenheim. He was 32. The Jim Clark Trust notes that there were no witnesses to the accident and describes a deflated rear tyre as the widely accepted explanation. His death ended the Lotus partnership only months after the South African victory.

evidence.locator: Opening paragraph: date, F2 event, no witnesses; subsequent tyre explanation
